review_approvals.actual_review_reason: An empty coordinate subset Z is allowed in the Jaco–Tollefson branch, but an accepted surface must have nonempty essential disk boundary. The zero vector in the Haken box is not accepted merely because it occurs in the finite list.
The crossing-free knot still has a positive triangulation bound C(n+1); n=0 does not mean an empty triangulation. Both surface searches reject the zero normal vector as a disk certificate.
The validated input has one knot component. A one-generator crossing-free presentation and one accepted disk witness are allowed; inputs with multiple components fail the explicit knot-code test.

Boundary here is the actual torus boundary of the exterior, not an endpoint of a numerical parameter interval. Acceptance tests the normal surface boundary and its meridional intersection before returning a certificate.

The searches traverse explicitly bounded finite integer vectors or finitely specified primitive rays and their disk tests. No arbitrary selection from an unspecified family of nonempty sets is part of this procedure.

Invalid planar incidences, nontransverse crossings, incompatible normal quadrilaterals and a zero ray are handled by validation or rejection. These are actual invalid-input/certificate branches, not silently admitted disks.
This item defines two finite searches and their acceptance tests; it does not state the forward half of a correctness equivalence between unknotting and arbitrary search output.
The procedure Definition does not claim that every unknot yields an accepted witness within these bounds. Completeness of either search is not an unstated converse of its acceptance rule.
The claim gives sharp asymptotic testing risks under an extremal-profile and small-maximal-weight regime, rather than an if-and-only-if characterization of all profile sequences.
No converse says that observing this risk limit forces the displayed profile or maximal-weight hypotheses. Those are sufficient hypotheses for the proved asymptotics.
A single normalized nonzero weight cannot satisfy max_j|w_j|→0. Thus the sharp central-limit conclusion is not asserted for a one-coordinate alternative merely by substituting its weight.
The vanishing maximal-weight condition and positive bounded u exclude a dominant-coordinate or zero-normalizer degeneration. The stated uniform approximation uses precisely those hypotheses.
The risk level is alpha in (0,1), not alpha=0 or1. The proof uses a left quantile and strict upper-tail rejection, which preserves the claimed level even when a finite-sample distribution has atoms.

The extremal profile is normalized to a positive finite u and its squared weights have nonzero total. An empty active profile cannot meet these hypotheses; no empty-alternative Gaussian limit is asserted.
The sharp asymptotic assumes u stays in a compact subset of (0,infinity). The exact zero-signal profile and the regime u→0 are not cases of this particular sharp-limit statement.

Countable Choice is explicitly assumed for the statistical interfaces. The extremal profile and its positive normalization are hypotheses; the proof does not select profiles from an unproved nonempty optimizer set.
This Definition specifies evaluation from supplied ribbon-category data; it does not characterize which arbitrary link functions arise from such a category.
No inverse reconstruction of a ribbon category from evaluated colored links is claimed. The invariance/evaluation conventions are not a biconditional classification.

One colored component and the tensor-unit color are legitimate inputs. The evaluation lands in End(1); it need not be identified with the coefficient field unless that additional category hypothesis is given.

Singular diagrams and vanishing framing fields are outside the framed-link input. Crossings and extrema are represented by the specified braiding and duality morphisms, including their identity cases.

The input is a closed framed link, so there are no free tangle endpoints requiring additional boundary objects. The framed Reidemeister conventions retain twists rather than erasing a framing at a diagram boundary.
A framing is nowhere zero; a zero normal vector field is not allowed framing data. A zero morphism in the category may evaluate a diagram to zero without making the construction undefined.

Colors and their specified dual/ribbon data are supplied on finitely many components. The stated Countable Choice interface for the evaluator is retained; it is not replaced by an unsupported choice-free existence claim.
The empty framed link is permitted: its ribbon diagram evaluates to the identity of the tensor unit. It is not a zero morphism merely because there are no colored components.

A finite family of zero disks imposes no pairwise or dual-sphere equations; those conditions are vacuous. The ambient connected based manifold is nevertheless nonempty, so empty disk data are not an empty ambient example.

The relative normal Euler obstruction may be zero; this is exactly the extension condition for the supplied boundary framing. Group-ring intersection zero is distinct from the identity coefficient1 required for a geometric dual.
For one disk, the duality equation is lambda(f_1,g_1)=1, not0. With no distinct disks the off-diagonal equations are vacuous, but the self-intersection and framing conditions remain.

The specified immersed-disk models allow transverse double points with algebraically controlled intersections, not arbitrary triple points or tangent singularities. A failed framing obstruction is not silently treated as framed.

The Definition says the relative Euler obstruction vanishes precisely when the fixed boundary normal framing extends. In the forward direction, zero obstruction is the defining obstruction-theoretic criterion for extension; it is not the disk-embedding theorem.

An extension of the given boundary framing has zero relative normal Euler obstruction by its defining obstruction construction. This is the actual local iff in the Definition, distinct from any characterization of good groups.

The disk boundary framing is prescribed on its boundary collar and the relative Euler obstruction tests extension across the whole disk. Proper disk boundary and interior transverse double points have different local models.
The disks, spheres, whiskers and framings are part of a finite supplied datum. The Definition of a good group does not itself construct such a datum for every arbitrary manifold.

The abelian peripheral curve L=1 is retained, so the reduced one-dimensional locus is not empty for this knot definition. Zero-dimensional nonabelian components are deliberately not factors of the A-polynomial.
M and L belong to C*, so zero eigenvalues are excluded. The defining polynomial is a nonzero reduced generator, not the zero polynomial, and isolated image points are omitted from its curve factor.
The abelian factor L−1 is present; thus the unit polynomial1 is not the ordinary A-polynomial under this convention. A single abelian curve is a legitimate remaining locus.
Repeated curve components are reduced and zero-dimensional images are discarded. This is why reducible representations or a lower-dimensional image are not counted with artificial multiplicity.
The peripheral torus supplies the ordered meridian and preferred longitude. These are marking data, not limits M=0 or L=0: both variables remain invertible Laurent variables.
The Definition explicitly equates retaining the abelian curve with divisibility by L−1 in the Laurent representative. A polynomial vanishing on every (M,1) has zero remainder on division by L−1.

Conversely an L−1 factor makes the representative vanish on the abelian peripheral curve. This equivalence concerns the retained factor, not a characterization of which Laurent polynomials are realized by knots.

The A-polynomial Definition assumes AC for its algebraic-geometry framework and fixes peripheral markings. No canonical representative is chosen from polynomial units without the stated primitive/normalization convention.
The empty closed oriented manifold is the zero bordism representative. Allowing it does not make X empty: X is assumed path connected with its CW-space convention.
Zero is represented by the empty manifold with its unique map to X. A nullbordism has boundary M and its map restricts to f; it is not obtained by setting the target map to a numeric zero.
The one-point target is allowed and recovers ordinary oriented bordism. A single connected source component is allowed, while disconnected representatives and disjoint-union addition are retained.

Disconnected and empty representatives are permitted; singular spaces are not substituted for the required closed smooth oriented source manifolds. Product bordisms supply reflexivity even for empty sources.

The bordism boundary is identified with M_0 disjoint union minus M_1, and the target map must restrict to the two given maps. Boundary orientation is part of the relation, not an optional endpoint sign.

The datum consists of one finite-dimensional manifold and one map; an asserted bordism includes its actual manifold, boundary identification and map. No indexed family of choices of representatives is made.
The item defines the bordism relation by existence of a marked bordism. It does not claim a separate forward characterization in terms of homology or homotopy invariants.
No homological condition is claimed sufficient for a bordism. The existence-of-W criterion is the defining relation, rather than an unproved converse classification theorem.
The attaching knot is an embedded circle and is not empty. The construction attaches one actual two-handle; the empty handle list would give B4 and is not the zero-trace input.
Zero denotes the framing relative to the preferred longitude, not omission of the two-handle or a zero-dimensional attaching region. The boundary is the corresponding zero surgery.
Exactly one two-handle is attached to B4 along the given knot. No multi-component link or one-dimensional handle is implicit in this trace Definition.
A singular attaching circle or a nonintegral unspecified framing is not accepted as a smooth handle attachment. Zero framing itself is regular, not a degenerate attachment.

The attaching collar lies in the boundary S3 and the remaining handle boundary becomes the surgery boundary after rounding corners. The framing identifies the longitude and hence the actual filled boundary.
Defining the trace and identifying its boundary surgery does not assert that a boundary homeomorphism forces the original attaching knots to agree.
No converse recovering K from an arbitrary four-manifold with zero-surgery boundary is claimed. The item only specifies the trace associated to the given K.

The knot and zero-framing convention determine the finite attachment datum up to the specified equivalence. No family of arbitrary framings is selected; the chosen tubular identification is part of a representative construction.
The examples calculate rates for specified singular-value sequences; they do not assert that only these operators can realize those rates.
A rate of this size is not claimed to imply polynomial or exponential singular-value asymptotics. The calculations use the displayed model as input.
The sequence model has infinitely many positive-mode coordinates; Q>0 and the Sobolev class are prescribed. It is not a minimax problem over an empty truth class or an empty frequency set.

The rates are as epsilon decreases through positive values. Substituting epsilon=0 into the logarithmic severe-ill-posed formula is not part of the claim, and Q=0 is excluded by the positive-radius hypothesis.
A single retained coefficient is not the infinite Sobolev minimax class. The dimension-dependent powers and exponential singular values are asserted for the full positive-index sequence model.
The displayed singular values are positive in the relevant modes. A zero singular value with an undetectable coefficient would violate this model rather than satisfy the same minimax calculation.

The severely ill-posed expression uses log(1/epsilon) for sufficiently small positive epsilon. The positive regularity and ill-posedness parameter restrictions are retained; no critical endpoint rate is inferred by continuity.
Countable Choice is explicitly retained for the Gaussian sequence/minimax framework. The supplied singular system and positive class radius are not selected from an unproved existence assertion.
For g=0 the Seifert matrix is empty and already the terminal matrix; its Alexander determinant is1. No nonempty primitive-kernel vector is demanded in this branch.
For positive genus, the unit Alexander polynomial forces det(V)=0 in the kernel-reduction step; zero determinant is the mechanism for lowering genus, not a forbidden nonsingular-matrix assumption.
Alexander polynomial1 means the unit class under the stated normalization. A one-handle Seifert form can be reduced by the same primitive-kernel construction; it is not a one-by-one Seifert matrix.

The proof deliberately permits a singular Seifert matrix while requiring the skew-symmetric intersection form to be unimodular. Conflating those two determinants would remove the very reduction case used.
This item proves Alexander-one implies S-equivalent to the empty form. It does not state the reverse as a separate characterization of arbitrary matrices beyond its Seifert hypotheses.
No conclusion that every algebraically slice Seifert form has Alexander polynomial1 is asserted. S-equivalence to the empty form is the output of the stronger unit-polynomial input.
The finite reduction stops at genus0, where no further kernel or band is selected. Genus is a nonnegative integer, not an interval parameter with an omitted boundary limit.
The positive-genus kernel step uses a primitive integer vector and finite integral basis operations under the stated AC framework. The g=0 branch makes no such selection.
Independence of the resulting Witt/signature invariant is not a criterion characterizing which characters extend over every bounding manifold.
The invariant comparison does not claim that equal signatures imply bordism equivalence. Only invariance and nonsingularity after the specified reduction are proved.
The AC assumption and actual finite bordism/character extensions are retained. A character is not assumed surjective onto an artificially fixed cyclic target;4.1 passes to its actual finite image.

Empty added closed bordism components contribute zero; the marked surgery/branched-cover boundary is still a nonempty input. The proof compares actual bounding multiples, not an empty boundary substituted for the knot data.
A single bounding copy r=1 may be used when it exists. In general r must be a positive bounding multiple, so no division by a zero number of copies occurs.

A constant character is admitted and its untwisted signature comparison is handled in1.1. At poles the signature is defined using the image/reduced nonsingular form rather than inverting a singular raw matrix.
The raw middle-dimensional intersection pairing may have a radical. Step3.1 passes to the appropriate image form before using nonsingularity, so zero or degenerate summands are not silently inverted.

The signature limit in5.1 is theta→0 from the positive side, chosen away from the finite exceptional set. It does not substitute a pole into a nonsingular form or identify two undefined endpoint signatures.
The theorem asserts existence and uniqueness up to color exchange for a connected regular projection; it does not characterize all embedded graphs admitting a checkerboard coloring.
A graph having a checkerboard coloring is not claimed to arise from the stipulated connected regular knot/link projection. That converse is not used.
Repeated edges and loops are accommodated by parity. Nonregular tangencies or non-4-valent crossings are not input regular-link diagrams and are not justified by the coloring proof.
A single crossing and graph loops do not obstruct parity coloring. The path-independence argument counts crossings modulo2 rather than assuming distinct edges or at least two crossings.

Paths used for coloring have endpoints in complementary regions and cross projection edges transversely. Endpoints on the graph or a crossing vertex are avoided by the prescribed local path perturbation.
The projection graph is connected and nonempty in the hypothesis. An empty projection is not an extra graph with two colorings; the proof fixes a complementary region of the actual diagram.

Choosing one region fixes which of the two colors it receives; finitely many region adjacencies then determine the rest. Connectedness of the dual adjacency graph gives exactly two choices, not an arbitrary coloring family.

A crossing-free circle is the familiar two-region coloring when represented as a regular diagram; no crossing sign is needed. In the finite graph argument the even-intersection parity, not a positive crossing count, controls consistency.
The boundary homology class lies in the longitude kernel, but essentiality excludes its being the zero primitive torus class. Consequently the coefficient k of the longitude is ±1 rather than0.
One actual essential disk suffices. Primitivity of its simple essential boundary curve forces longitude multiplicity1 in absolute value; the proof does not assume a family of parallel disks.
A boundary circle that is inessential in the torus would have class0 and is explicitly excluded. The proof uses that exclusion before concluding that its longitudinal multiple is primitive.
Properness places the disk boundary on the exterior torus and its interior off that torus. The longitude conclusion concerns this boundary marking, not an arbitrary interior loop.
An essential properly embedded disk has an actual nonempty boundary circle on the exterior torus. Neither an empty surface nor a closed disk away from that boundary meets the premise.
Longitudinal homology alone is not claimed sufficient for an essential disk. In particular no unknot conclusion is obtained merely from the existence of the longitude marking.
The disk is supplied by the hypothesis. Its finite homology calculation and a meridian representative require no selection from all possible essential disks.
The assertion is that an essential disk boundary has longitude slope. It does not say that every longitude curve on every knot exterior bounds a disk.
Matching and quadrilateral constraints are checked before disk acceptance. An incompatible normal vector or a closed sphere of Euler characteristic2 does not pass the disk tests.
The candidate boundary lies in the exterior boundary torus. Its odd meridian intersection excludes a nullhomologous boundary there, giving the essential-boundary condition actually required.

The accepted candidate has nonempty boundary and disk Euler characteristic. The empty normal surface cannot meet the acceptance tests, even though zero coordinates belong to the ambient bounded enumeration.
The zero normal vector fails the nonempty disk-boundary test. Odd meridional intersection of an accepted candidate is also nonzero and is used to establish essentiality.
The conclusion applies to one accepted Haken candidate, including a disk with a single boundary component. It makes no claim that multiple accepted disks must agree.
Existence of an essential disk is not here shown to force this finite search to accept. Only an already accepted normal vector is interpreted geometrically.
The acceptance witness is already given by the algorithm premise. The proof need not choose an accepted candidate from an unexplored infinite surface class.
This lemma proves soundness of the Haken acceptance branch. It does not prove the converse search-completeness assertion or soundness of an unrelated Jaco–Tollefson branch.
The second-moment computation supplies lower bounds on testing risk from a given mixture; it does not characterize every experiment with the same risk.
A small testing risk is not claimed to imply failure of this mixture construction. These are sufficient mixture lower-bound estimates, not a converse criterion.
For one active coordinate the Rademacher mixture has the displayed single cosh likelihood and the second-moment estimate remains valid. No central-limit small-maximal-weight condition is needed here.

Some coordinates of v may vanish; their likelihood factors are1. The finite nonzero fourth-moment normalization is controlled by the separated-profile premise, not by an assumption that every listed coordinate is nonzero.
The testing risk convention fixes alpha in (0,1) and epsilon>0. No division by zero noise or endpoint normal quantile is made in the mixture inequality.

The inherited separation radius r is positive and v belongs to the separated alternative, so its finite active support J cannot be empty. Formally the empty likelihood product would be1 and u=0, but that is not an admissible separated profile.
Zero individual v_j entries contribute cosh(0)=1 and do not invalidate the finite product bound. The all-zero profile is excluded by v in Theta_q(r) with r>0; epsilon remains positive.

Only finitely many independent signs are mixed on the given finite J; Countable Choice is retained for the surrounding Gaussian sequence model. The argument does not need to choose a new extremal alternative.
Well-definedness says changing permitted construction choices preserves the resulting knot class; it does not classify all decompositions of a knot into prime summands.
Equal connected-sum results are not asserted to imply equal summands or identical gluing data. Cancellation and prime decomposition are not conclusions of this lemma.
Each input knot is a nonempty oriented circle; a zero-crossing unknot is allowed. An empty link is not one of the two summands, so deleting a summand is not a hidden empty-input operation.

A small standard ball has positive radius and a genuine embedded arc. Singular arcs or a chart transition reversing the required orientation are not admitted choices in the well-definedness statement.
The operation takes two knots; if one is an unknot its local arc and collar still exist. It is not defined by choosing one special crossing or requiring a nontrivial knot.
Countable Choice is retained for the stated isotopy interfaces. The proof uses finitely many supplied chart/arc choices and compares them by the actual compact isotopy-extension argument.
Zero crossings cause no problem because the construction removes a standard local arc, not a crossing. The chart rescaling includes its derivative-limit value at scale0 as specified in1.2.

The removed arc endpoints are matched with the specified oriented standard collars. Transition maps must respect that orientation; an orientation-reversing arbitrary gluing is not an equivalent marked connected sum.

Finite cellular chain blocks may have rank0 and give zero Hilbert modules; cap duality and weak exactness then have their zero-space interpretation. The actual compact manifold/group datum is not replaced by missing chain complexes.
Zero reduced homology and zero projections are allowed. Kernels and closures of images, rather than an inverse of a zero or nonclosed map, define the reduced Hilbert statements.
The trivial group and rank-one free cellular blocks are permitted. Their von Neumann-module reductions specialize to the ordinary Hilbert/cellular calculation without a nontrivial-group hypothesis.

A nonclosed operator range is handled by its closure, and pairing radicals are removed before duality. An algebraically exact sequence is not silently promoted to a sequence of closed-range isomorphisms.

For manifold pairs, the boundary and relative chain blocks use the displayed cap-product conventions. Weak exactness means equality after taking the specified closures, not surjectivity at an omitted endpoint term.
The Statement explicitly assumes AC for its Hilbert-module framework. Finite CW structures and actual chain maps are inputs; no choice-free strengthening is inferred from finite cell counts.
The asserted dualities and weak exactness are properties of the supplied cellular L2 construction, not an iff test for whether a manifold has a given group.
Vanishing L2 homology is not claimed to determine the underlying topology or imply the geometric hypotheses. Only the stated analytic/cellular consequences are used.
The surface is connected and has its nonempty longitudinal boundary in the knot exterior. The empty surface cannot satisfy these hypotheses or serve as a fiber representative.
Genus0 is included: the disk-fiber case is handled in3.1 instead of invoking positive-genus surface-group arguments. No nonzero rank is required of the disk fundamental group.
One connected nonseparating incompressible longitudinal surface is the input. The theorem does not require several parallel fibers or two independent boundary components.

Separating or compressible surfaces are excluded, because the covering/surface-group argument uses nonseparation and incompressibility. The disk fiber is a genuine included case rather than such a degeneration.

The proper boundary curves have the specified longitude marking; the isotopy to a fiber respects the aligned boundary convention. There is no free choice of a different peripheral slope at the boundary.
The fibered exterior, surface and markings are supplied under the stated AC assumption. The proof compares this surface with an existing fiber; it does not select a fibration from all knot exteriors.
In a given fibered exterior the stated longitudinal incompressible surface is identified with a fiber. No converse says existence of any longitudinal surface alone makes the knot fibered.
The theorem does not classify nonfibered exteriors by failure of a particular surface isotopy. Fiberedness is a hypothesis throughout.
This constructs one rational ball with the displayed lens-space boundary, not a classification of which lens spaces bound rational balls.
A rational filling of some lens space is not claimed to force the conic construction or the same integral homology. No such converse is used.
The conic is an actual nonempty embedded S2 with a disk-bundle neighborhood. Its complement is not obtained by removing an empty set from the ambient manifold.
There is one connected boundary lens space L(4,1) with the stated orientation convention. It is not the trivial lens space S3 obtained by replacing4 with1.
The conic is nonsingular and its normal Euler number is4 rather than0. A reducible or singular conic would not give the embedded sphere used in the disk-bundle construction.
Positive-degree rational homology vanishes, while H0 is Q. The integral Z/2 phenomenon is retained, so rational-ball terminology does not assert integral acyclicity.

The normal circle bundle has Euler number4, computed from the actual transition function. The induced boundary orientation is tracked; the result is not an orientation-free equality of surgery coefficients.
The AC framework and explicit conic/tubular-neighborhood data are retained. A rational homology computation does not choose or assert an arbitrary filling for every lens space.
The claim constructs a definite closed four-manifold from supplied slicing and filling data; it does not characterize all definite four-manifolds as such gluings.
Existence of the resulting definite form is not asserted sufficient for sliceness. The logical direction is the obstruction-producing construction from a slice disk.
The branching disk and its boundary knot are nonempty, and the cover has its given boundary M. Empty branching would be a different unbranched construction and is not covered.
The construction is a double branched cover with one marked rational-homology-sphere gluing boundary, not a variable number of sheets. A single supplied positive-definite filling is enough.

The rational-homology-sphere and normal-generation conditions are essential: the proof uses them to remove extra middle homology and the fundamental group. They are not dropped in a degenerate boundary case.
Rank-zero b2 is allowed: positive definiteness of the zero intersection form is vacuous, and Mayer–Vietoris still gives the displayed b2 formula. The proof never divides by that rank.
The cover piece is glued with reversed boundary orientation along M using actual collars. This boundary marking is what permits the homology and normal-generation pi1 arguments.
The AC assumption and given smooth filling/branching data are retained. The theorem constructs from those data and does not assert existence of a positive-definite filling for every cover.
The normalized complex has a specified nonzero total homology generator, so the admissible cycle family used to define tau is not empty. A zero complex is not an admitted marked knot complex.
Extra acyclic terms are harmless only through the stated filtered homotopies; an empty total generator or an arbitrary multipointed factor is not normalized by fiat.
The theorem proves diagram independence of a normalized integer, not a characterization of knots having a specified tau value.
Equal tau values are not claimed to imply equivalence of Heegaard diagrams, knots or filtered complexes. The assertion only compares diagrams of the same marked knot.
Setting extra basepoint variables to zero is performed on polynomial chain maps and homotopies. This is a literal specialization identity, not an unjustified assertion that every quotient is flat.
The filtration origin is fixed by the marked Seifert normalization on both diagrams. Equality of relative filtrations without that origin would not determine the same integer tau.
Countable Choice and the supplied finite pointed move comparisons are retained. The total-generator normalization rules out choosing an arbitrary nonzero class in an unspecified homology group.
A singly pointed-pair knot has no extra V factor; its distinguished factor is the unit. The comparison does not manufacture an extra exterior-generator summand in this case.
At genus0 the Seifert matrix and compression list are empty, and the existing Seifert disk is the required disk. The knot itself remains a nonempty circle.
Zero genus is handled separately in1.1. The Alexander hypothesis is the unit polynomial1, not a zero polynomial or a vanishing determinant interpreted as that polynomial.
A single Seifert handle is permitted and enters the same finite reduction. Polynomial1 is a unit class; it does not mean the degree-one polynomial t−1.
Empty handle data at genus0 are legitimate. In positive genus the unimodular Seifert-intersection conditions are preserved; an arbitrary singular surface is not admitted as a Seifert disk.
The theorem gives the sufficient condition Delta=1 for topological sliceness. It does not state that every topologically slice knot has trivial Alexander polynomial.
The reverse implication topologically slice⇒Alexander polynomial1 is not asserted. The one-way disk construction must not be upgraded to that false classification.

The construction retains the actual boundary knot collar and its normal framing. The resulting disk is locally flat topological; smoothness is not inferred at the boundary from the topological disk theorem.
The Statement explicitly assumes full AC for the imported topological disk machinery. No Countable-Choice-only or choice-free strengthening is made by this boundary disposition.
The claim ranges over actual Newton edges of the retained curve polynomial. A zero-length vector or an omitted zero-dimensional representation component is not an edge to which a slope is assigned.
The edge normal is a nonzero integral vector, defined up to sign. A zero valuation pair would not define its boundary slope and is not used as a primitive edge normal.
One actual edge is enough to obtain the associated essential surface. No minimum number of nonabelian factors or two independent edge directions is assumed.

Reducible representations and isolated image points are treated by the ordinary reduced A-polynomial convention. The proof does not assume a generic smooth point represents every exceptional boundary value.
Vertical edge data are allowed and correspond to the infinite slope convention rather than division by zero. The boundary slope is a peripheral class, not an endpoint value of a real interval.
Full AC and the supplied algebraic-curve/ideal-point framework are explicit. The finite extension/valuation choices are made for the chosen edge, not asserted to be canonical for every polynomial.
Every Newton edge slope is shown to be a boundary slope; not every boundary slope is claimed to occur on the ordinary A-polynomial Newton polygon.
No converse realizes an arbitrary essential-surface boundary slope as a Newton edge. The edge-to-surface construction is the stated direction.
The trivial input group is allowed, but its mitosis still includes the specified stable letters. An empty bar-chain support is filled by zero; it is not a missing nonempty generator choice.
Acyclicity here is vanishing in positive degrees; H0 remains Z. The construction does not call a nonempty connected classifying space reduced-acyclic by setting its ordinary H0 to zero.

The identity group and degree-one cycles are included in the formulas. Group identity labels are multiplicative1, distinct from the zero chain; normalized degenerate simplices are handled before claiming a filling.
Identity-labelled degenerate bar simplices are included in the normalization discussion. Their treatment is necessary to distinguish a normalized zero chain from an unaccounted nonzero boundary.
The construction uses the discrete stages G→m(G)→… and their union, with explicit transition embeddings. It is not a continuous parameter family requiring a limit-time homeomorphism.

Full AC is stated. Each individual bar cycle has finite support and the proof gives finite fillings at a sufficiently advanced stage; it does not invoke an unspecified simultaneous choice of all fillings.
The functorial construction embeds each group into an acyclic envelope; it does not characterize which groups were already acyclic.
Acyclicity of the envelope is not claimed to imply acyclicity of its subgroup. Naturality and injectivity of the construction do not give that converse.

The group extension has its identity elements and connected classifying spaces, so there is no empty base or fiber. Empty higher-degree chain groups can still yield zero entries on a spectral-sequence diagonal.
The p=0 and q=0 edges belong to the first quadrant; H0 of the identity group is Z rather than0. At total degree0 only E2_(0,0) contributes.
Either N=1 or Q=1 is allowed and gives the corresponding trivial-extension specialization. The usual identity coefficients and collapsed positive-degree homology are retained.
Trivial kernels or quotients are legitimate. Surjectivity of G→Q and identification of N with its kernel are retained; a nonexact sequence is not treated as a degenerate extension.
Exactness at the two identity-group ends of 1→N→G→Q→1 is part of the input extension. The filtration of H_n has its actual finite first and last terms, not an omitted convergence endpoint.
An exact group extension produces the spectral sequence. The theorem does not characterize all spectral sequences as arising from extensions.
Existence of groups with the displayed E2 terms does not assert an extension realizing them. No converse extension construction follows from convergence alone.

Full AC is explicitly part of the stated group-homology framework. The extension maps and module actions are given data; a section is not assumed to be a homomorphism or chosen without its stated framework.
The result establishes the monoid laws, not a criterion that detects whether two arbitrary connected-sum decompositions are equal.
Commutativity and associativity do not assert cancellation, inverses or prime uniqueness. Those converse/cancellation claims are absent.
The knots are nonempty circles. The empty product convention of a monoid, when used, is the unknot identity, not an empty embedded link.
The unknot is included and gives the unit; singular knots and empty links are outside the smooth oriented knot domain. No inverse knot is asserted in this monoid theorem.
The two-sided unit proof covers K#unknot and unknot#K. Thus a product with one nonunit factor retains that knot class.

The stated Countable Choice interfaces for knot isotopy and connected-sum well-definedness are retained. A finite product is handled by finite composition, not arbitrary representatives of every knot class.
The standard arc collars and their oriented endpoint pairings are retained under the half-turn and associativity isotopies. No interval-endpoint limit is used to exchange factors.
A crossing-free unknot represents the identity class, not a zero knot with empty underlying set. The identity gluing uses its actual standard arc and ball.
The formula computes the genus of the constructed Seifert surface and hence an upper bound for knot genus. It does not say that every Seifert surface is genus-minimizing.
A numerical genus upper bound is not claimed to characterize which diagrams realize a knot or when the Seifert algorithm is optimal.
For a crossing-free knot the crossing list is empty, but there is one Seifert circle and one disk. The surface is not empty and its genus formula gives0.
Repeated visits to a Seifert circle are permitted, but the final surface is connected with one boundary component. Only pairs (s,c) realized by that construction enter the integer genus formula.
The boundary is exactly the oriented input knot after band attachment and rounding. Its being one component is essential in converting Euler characteristic to 1−2g.
One crossing is allowed. For example c=1,s=2 gives genus0; the one-boundary orientable-surface condition prevents treating c=1,s=1 as an admissible half-integral genus case.
The finite oriented diagram supplies its Seifert circles and crossing bands under the stated Countable Choice framework. No global choice of a minimal-genus surface is required.
c=0 and connected one-knot boundary force s=1 in this construction, so g=(0−1+1)/2=0. The formula is not applied to an arbitrary empty link with s=0.
Additivity, mirror symmetry and the genus inequality are not a criterion characterizing slice knots by Upsilon=0.
Vanishing Upsilon is not asserted sufficient for smooth sliceness. Nor is equality in its genus bound claimed to determine the knot.
At t=0 the normalized ordinary tower gives Upsilon0=0. If the four-ball genus is0, the stated bound on [0,1] forces Upsilon to vanish there and symmetry gives vanishing on the remaining half.
Reflection t↔2−t and Upsilon(0)=0 give Upsilon(2)=0. The derivative formula uses the right derivative at0; no two-sided derivative or an unproved differentiability at every corner is asserted.

The Countable Choice and exact source-qualified filtered-complex inputs remain explicit. The minimum is taken over representatives of the existing generator, not over an assumed nonempty family for an arbitrary acyclic complex.
The defining infinity homology has the normalized tower generator, so its representing-cycle set is nonempty. The zero complex is not an admitted replacement for the knot complex.
The value t=1 lies in the stated closed genus-bound interval. Additivity applies to two knots even when either is the unknot, whose normalized complex supplies the unit.
Acyclic summands or repeated affine minimizers may produce corners but do not remove the tower class. The genus estimate is used only on its declared t interval, then extended by the stated symmetry.
